<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document" style="font-size:144%;">DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname"><span id="id1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">
Zhihong Shao*, Yuxiang Luo*, Chengda Lu*<sup id="id1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">†</span></sup>, Z.Z. Ren*
Jiewen Hu, Tian Ye, Zhibin Gou, Shirong Ma, Xiaokang Zhang
<span id="id1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">DeepSeek-AI
zhihongshao@deepseek.com 
<br class="ltx_break"><a href="https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-Math-V2" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-Math-V2</a>

</span></span>
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_correspondent"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Corresponding author: </span>Core contributors   <sup id="id2" class="ltx_sup"><span id="id2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">†</span></sup>Work done during internship at DeepSeek-AI.
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models have made significant progress in mathematical reasoning, which serves as an important testbed for AI and could impact scientific research if further advanced.
By scaling reasoning with reinforcement learning that rewards correct final answers, LLMs have improved from poor performance to saturating quantitative reasoning competitions like AIME and HMMT in one year.
However, this approach faces fundamental limitations.
Pursuing higher final answer accuracy doesn’t address a key issue: correct answers don’t guarantee correct reasoning.
Moreover, many mathematical tasks like theorem proving require rigorous step-by-step derivation rather than numerical answers, making final answer rewards inapplicable.
To push the limits of deep reasoning, we believe it is necessary to verify the comprehensiveness and rigor of mathematical reasoning.
Self-verification is particularly important for scaling test-time compute, especially for open problems without known solutions.
Towards self-verifiable mathematical reasoning, we investigate how to train an accurate and faithful LLM-based verifier for theorem proving.
We then train a proof generator using the verifier as the reward model, and incentivize the generator to identify and resolve as many issues as possible in their own proofs before finalizing them.
To maintain the generation-verification gap as the generator becomes stronger, we propose to scale verification compute to automatically label new hard-to-verify proofs, creating training data to further improve the verifier.
Our resulting model, DeepSeekMath-V2, demonstrates strong theorem-proving capabilities, achieving gold-level scores on IMO 2025 and CMO 2024 and a near-perfect 118/120 on Putnam 2024 with scaled test-time compute.
While much work remains, these results suggest that self-verifiable mathematical reasoning is a feasible research direction that may help develop more capable mathematical AI systems.</p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The conventional approach to reinforcement learning (RL) for mathematical reasoning involves rewarding large language models (LLMs) based on whether their predicted final answers to quantitative reasoning problems match ground-truth answers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.
This methodology suffices to allow frontier LLMs to saturate mathematical competitions that primarily evaluate final answers, such as AIME and HMMT.
However, this reward mechanism has two fundamental limitations.
First, it serves as an unreliable proxy for reasoning correctness – a model can arrive at the correct answer through flawed logic or fortunate errors.
Second, it is inapplicable to theorem proving tasks, where problems may not require producing numerical final answers and rigorous derivation is the primary objective.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Consequently, LLMs trained on quantitative reasoning problems with such final answer reward still frequently produce mathematically invalid or logically inconsistent natural-language proofs.
Moreover, this training approach does not naturally develop the models’ ability to verify proof validity – they exhibit high false-positive rates, often claiming incorrect proofs are valid even when they contain obvious logical flaws.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The lack of a generation-verification gap in natural-language theorem proving hinders further improvement.
To address this, we propose developing proof verification capabilities in LLMs.
Our approach is motivated by several key observations:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Humans can identify issues in proofs even without reference solutions – a crucial ability when tackling open problems.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A proof is more likely to be valid when no issues can be identified despite scaled verification efforts.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The efforts required to identify valid issues can serve as a proxy for proof quality, which can be exploited to optimize proof generation.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">We believe that LLMs can be trained to identify proof issues without reference solutions.
Such a verifier would enable an iterative improvement cycle: (1) using verification feedback to optimize proof generation, (2) scaling verification compute to auto-label hard-to-verify new proofs, thereby creating the training data to improve the verifier itself, and (3) using this enhanced verifier to further optimize proof generation.
Moreover, a reliable proof verifier enables us to teach proof generators to evaluate proofs as the verifier does.
This allows a proof generator to iteratively refine its proofs until it can no longer identify or resolve any issues.
In essence, we make the model explicitly aware of its reward function and enable it to maximize this reward through deliberate reasoning rather than blind trial-and-error.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Built on DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp-Base <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2025</a>)</cite>, we developed <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DeepSeekMath-V2</span>, a large language model optimized for natural-language theorem proving that demonstrates self-verifiable mathematical reasoning.
Our model can assess and iteratively improve its own proofs, achieving gold-level performance in premier high-school mathematics competitions including IMO 2025 and CMO 2024.
On the Putnam 2024 undergraduate competition, it scored 118/120, exceeding the highest score of 90 <span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
            
            
            
          <a href="https://kskedlaya.org/putnam-archive/putnam2024stats.html" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://kskedlaya.org/putnam-archive/putnam2024stats.html</a></span></span></span> obtained by human participants.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Method</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Proof Verification</h3>

<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.1.1 </span>Training a Verifier to Identify Issues and Score Proofs</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We developed high-level rubrics <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{v}</annotation></semantics></math> for proof evaluation (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS2" title="A.2 Proof Verification Prompt ‣ Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.2</span></a>) with the goal of training a verifier to evaluate proofs according to these rubrics, mirroring mathematical experts’ assessment process.
Specifically, given a problem <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> and a proof <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math>, the verifier <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\pi_{\varphi}(\cdot|{}X,Y,\mathcal{I}_{v})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>φ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\varphi}(\cdot|{}X,Y,\mathcal{I}_{v})</annotation></semantics></math> is designed to produce a proof analysis that first summarizes identified issues (if any) and then assigns a score based on three levels:
1 for complete and rigorous proofs with all logical steps clearly justified;
0.5 for proofs with sound overall logic but minor errors or omitted details;
and 0 for fundamentally flawed proofs containing fatal logical errors or critical gaps.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Curating Cold Start RL Data</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We constructed our initial training data through the following process:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S2.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We crawled problems from Art of Problem Solving (AoPS) contests <span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
                        <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
                        
                        
                        
                      <a href="https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c13_contest_collections" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c13_contest_collections</a></span></span></span>, prioritizing math olympiads, team selection tests, and post-2010 problems explicitly requiring proofs, totaling 17,503 problems.
This problem set is denoted as <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We generated candidate proofs using a variant of DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp-Thinking. As this model was not optimized for theorem proving and tended to produce concise but error-prone outputs, we prompted it to iteratively refine its proofs over multiple rounds to improve comprehensiveness and rigor.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We randomly sampled proofs across diverse problem types (e.g., algebra and number theory) and had mathematical experts score each proof according to the evaluation rubrics described above.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This process yielded an initial RL dataset <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{v}=\{(X_{i},Y_{i},s_{i})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{v}=\{(X_{i},Y_{i},s_{i})\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where each item consists of a problem <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, a proof <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>, and an overall proof score <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}\in\{0,0.5,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}\in\{0,0.5,1\}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">RL Objective.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Building on a version of DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp-SFT which was supervised fine-tuned on reasoning data related to mathematics and code, we trained the model with reinforcement learning to produce proof analyses using two reward components:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S2.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Format reward</span> <math id="S2.I2.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{format}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>format</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{format}}</annotation></semantics></math>: An indicator function that enforces the model to generate both a summary of identified issues and a proof score, by checking whether the final response contains the key phrase “Here is my evaluation of the solution:” as well as a score within <span id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">\boxed{}</span> following “Based on my evaluation, the final overall score should be:”.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Score reward</span> <math id="S2.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{score}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>score</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{score}}</annotation></semantics></math>: Rewards based on proximity between predicted score <math id="S2.I2.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> and annotated score <math id="S2.I2.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="S2.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{score}}(s_{i}^{\prime},s_{i})=1-|s_{i}^{\prime}-s_{i}|" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>score</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>−</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{score}}(s_{i}^{\prime},s_{i})=1-|s_{i}^{\prime}-s_{i}|</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The RL objective for training the verifier is:</p>
<table id="S2.E2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\max_{\pi_{\varphi}}\mathbb{E}_{(X_{i},Y_{i},s_{i})\sim\mathcal{D}_{v},(V_{i}^{\prime},s_{i}^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\varphi}(\cdot|X_{i},Y_{i})}\left[R_{\text{format}}(V_{i}^{\prime})\cdot R_{\text{score}}(s_{i}^{\prime},s_{i})\right]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>φ</mi></msub></munder><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>v</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mrow></mrow><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>∼</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>φ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>X</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo>[</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>format</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>score</mtext></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{\pi_{\varphi}}\mathbb{E}_{(X_{i},Y_{i},s_{i})\sim\mathcal{D}_{v},(V_{i}^{\prime},s_{i}^{\prime})\sim\pi_{\varphi}(\cdot|X_{i},Y_{i})}\left[R_{\text{format}}(V_{i}^{\prime})\cdot R_{\text{score}}(s_{i}^{\prime},s_{i})\right]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(2)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{i}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{i}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the verifier’s final response and <math id="S2.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>′</mo></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math> is the proof score extracted from it.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.1.2 </span>Introducing Meta-Verification to Review Proof Analyses</h4>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The approach described in Section <a href="#S2.SS1.SSS1" title="2.1.1 Training a Verifier to Identify Issues and Score Proofs ‣ 2.1 Proof Verification ‣ 2 Method ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1.1</span></a> trains proof verification through RL to align predicted proof scores with expert annotations, but provides no direct supervision on the identified issues themselves.
This creates a critical vulnerability: when evaluating flawed proofs (where <math id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{i}&lt;1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{i}&lt;1</annotation></semantics></math>) during training, the verifier can receive full reward by predicting the correct scores while hallucinating non-existent issues, undermining its trustworthiness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To address this problem, we introduce <span id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">meta-verification</span>: a secondary evaluation process that assesses whether issues identified by the verifier indeed exist and whether these issues logically justify the predicted proof score according to the evaluation rubrics <math id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{v}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The complete meta-verification rubrics <math id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{mv}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{mv}</annotation></semantics></math> are detailed in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Meta-Verification Prompt ‣ Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We trained a dedicated meta-verifier using RL to perform this evaluation.
By incorporating the meta-verifier’s feedback into verifier training, we can improve the faithfulness of the verifier’s issue identification.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Meta-Verifier Training Process</h5>

<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S2.I3" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We obtained an initial verifier <math id="S2.I3.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\varphi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>φ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\varphi}</annotation></semantics></math> following Section <a href="#S2.SS1.SSS1" title="2.1.1 Training a Verifier to Identify Issues and Score Proofs ‣ 2.1 Proof Verification ‣ 2 Method ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1.1</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Mathematical experts scored the quality of verifier responses according to <math id="S2.I3.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{mv}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{mv}</annotation></semantics></math>, creating dataset <math id="S2.I3.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{mv}=\{(X_{i},Y_{i},V_{i},ms_{i})\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{mv}=\{(X_{i},Y_{i},V_{i},ms_{i})\}</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S2.I3.i2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is the analysis of proof <math id="S2.I3.i2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.I3.i2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="ms_{i}\in\{0,0.5,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">ms_{i}\in\{0,0.5,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> is the expert-annotated quality score.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We trained a meta-verifier <math id="S2.I3.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\pi_{\eta}(\cdot|X,Y,V,\mathcal{I}_{mv})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\eta}(\cdot|X,Y,V,\mathcal{I}_{mv})</annotation></semantics></math> to analyze the verifier’s proof analysis <math id="S2.I3.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>V</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V</annotation></semantics></math>.
The meta-verifier produces a summary of issues found in the analysis itself, followed by a quality score measuring how accurate and justified the verifier’s analysis is.
The RL objective follows the same structure as the verifier training, with format and score rewards.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Using the trained meta-verifier <math id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\eta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>η</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\eta}</annotation></semantics></math>, we enhanced the verifier training by integrating meta-verification feedback into the reward function:</p>
<table id="S2.E3" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{V}=R_{\text{format}}\cdot R_{\text{score}}\cdot R_{\text{meta}}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>format</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>score</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>meta</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{V}=R_{\text{format}}\cdot R_{\text{score}}\cdot R_{\text{meta}}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(3)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{meta}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>meta</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{meta}}</annotation></semantics></math> is the quality score from the meta-verifier.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We trained the enhanced verifier on both the verification dataset <math id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{v}</annotation></semantics></math> and the meta-verification dataset <math id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{mv}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{mv}</annotation></semantics></math>, using the same reward mechanism on <math id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{mv}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{mv}</annotation></semantics></math> as used for training the meta-verifier.
The resulting model can perform both proof verification and meta-verification tasks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">On a validation split of <math id="S2.SS1.SSS2.Px1.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{D}_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{D}_{v}</annotation></semantics></math>, the average quality score of the verifier’s proof analyses – as evaluated by the meta-verifier – improved from 0.85 to 0.96, while maintaining the same accuracy in proof score prediction.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Proof Generation</h3>

<section id="S2.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.1 </span>Training a Generator for Theorem Proving</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">With verifier <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\varphi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>φ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\varphi}</annotation></semantics></math> serving as a generative reward model, we train a proof generator <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|{}X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|{}X)</annotation></semantics></math> with the RL objective:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.E4" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S2.E4.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\max_{\pi_{\theta}}\mathbb{E}_{X_{i}\sim\mathcal{D}_{p},Y_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|X_{i})}[R_{Y}]" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub></munder><msub><mi>𝔼</mi><mrow><mi>X</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒟</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>Y</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∼</mo><mi>π</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>X</mi><msub><mrow></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\max_{\pi_{\theta}}\mathbb{E}_{X_{i}\sim\mathcal{D}_{p},Y_{i}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|X_{i})}[R_{Y}]</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(4)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{Y}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{Y}</annotation></semantics></math> is the proof score produced by <math id="S2.SS2.SSS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\pi_{\varphi}(\cdot|{}X_{i},Y_{i},\mathcal{I}_{v})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>φ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>Y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\varphi}(\cdot|{}X_{i},Y_{i},\mathcal{I}_{v})</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.2.2 </span>Enhancing Reasoning via Self-Verification</h4>

<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When a proof generator fails to produce a completely correct proof in one shot – common for challenging problems from competitions like IMO and CMO – iterative verification and refinement can improve results.
This involves analyzing the proof with an external verifier and prompting the generator to address identified issues.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, we observed a critical limitation: when prompted to both generate and analyze its own proof in one shot, the generator tends to claim correctness even when the external verifier easily identify flaws.
In other words, while the generator can refine proofs based on external feedback, it fails to evaluate its own work with the same rigor as the dedicated verifier.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This observation motivated us to endow the proof generator with genuine verification capabilities.
During training, we prompt the generator <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> to produce a proof <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> followed by a self-analysis <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> that follows the same format and rubrics <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{I}_{v}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℐ</mi><mi>v</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{I}_{v}</annotation></semantics></math> as the verifier (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS1" title="A.1 Proof Generation Prompt ‣ Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.1</span></a>).
We denote the proof score predicted in the self-analysis as <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s^{\prime}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s^{\prime}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure faithful self-evaluation, we use the verifier <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\varphi}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>φ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\varphi}</annotation></semantics></math> to assess both components: the proof <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Y" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Y</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Y</annotation></semantics></math> receives score <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{Y}=s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{Y}=s</annotation></semantics></math>, and the self-analysis <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Z" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Z</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Z</annotation></semantics></math> receives a meta-verification score <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{meta}}(Z)=ms" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>meta</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{meta}}(Z)=ms</annotation></semantics></math>.
The reward function combines these assessments:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<table id="S2.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S2.E5"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle R</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=R_{\text{format}}(Y,Z)\cdot(\alpha\cdot R_{Y}+\beta\cdot R_{Z})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>format</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Y</mi></msub></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=R_{\text{format}}(Y,Z)\cdot(\alpha\cdot R_{Y}+\beta\cdot R_{Z})</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(5)</span></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S2.E6"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle R_{Z}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>Z</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle R_{Z}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S2.E6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=R_{\text{score}}(s^{\prime},s)\cdot R_{\text{meta}}(Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>score</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>meta</mtext></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=R_{\text{score}}(s^{\prime},s)\cdot R_{\text{meta}}(Z)</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(6)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{format}}(Y,Z)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>format</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{format}}(Y,Z)</annotation></semantics></math> verifies that both the proof and self-analysis follow the specified format, <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{score}}(s^{\prime},s)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>score</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{score}}(s^{\prime},s)</annotation></semantics></math> rewards accurate self-assessment.
We set <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p5.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.76" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.76</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.76</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS2.SSS2.p5.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta=0.24" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>β</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.24</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta=0.24</annotation></semantics></math>.
This reward structure creates the following incentives:</p>
<ul id="S2.I4" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Faithful acknowledgment of errors is rewarded over false claims of correctness.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I4.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The highest rewards come from producing correct proofs and accurately recognizing their rigor.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I4.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I4.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A good strategy to obtain high rewards for the proof generator is to identify and resolve as many issues as possible before finalizing the response.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Synergy Between Proof Verification and Generation</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The proof verifier and generator create a synergistic cycle:
the verifier improves the generator, and as the generator improves, it produces new proofs that challenge the verifier’s current capabilities.
These challenging cases – where the verifier may fail to identify issues in a single attempt – become valuable training data for enhancing the verifier itself.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To retrain and improve the verifier, we need labeled correctness data for newly generated proofs.
Manual annotation, while straightforward, becomes increasingly time-consuming as problems grow harder and errors become more subtle.
To boost annotation efficiency, we generated multiple verifier analyses per proof to surface potential issues for human review.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">From this AI-assisted annotation process, we recognized two facts that make it feasible to push the level of automation a step further:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S2.I5" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I5.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I5.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I5.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Scaling verifier samples increases the probability of catching real issues in flawed proofs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I5.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I5.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I5.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reviewing the verifier’s identified issues is exactly <span id="S2.I5.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">meta-verification</span>, which is easier than identifying issues from scratch. Meta-verification is also more sample-efficient for LLMs to master.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S2.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Building on these observations, we developed the following automated labeling process:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<ol id="S2.I6" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I6.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I6.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I6.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each proof, generate <math id="S2.I6.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> independent verification analyses</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I6.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I6.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I6.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For analyses reporting issues (scores 0 or 0.5), generate <math id="S2.I6.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math> meta-verification assessments to validate the identified problems.
An analysis is deemed valid if the majority of meta-assessments confirm its findings</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I6.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S2.I6.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I6.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each proof, we examine analyses that assign the lowest score.
If at least <math id="S2.I6.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> such analyses are deemed valid, the proof is labeled with that lowest score.
If no legitimate issues are identified across all verification attempts, the proof is labeled with 1.
Otherwise, the proof is discarded or routed to human experts for labeling</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
<p id="S2.SS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In our last two training iterations, this fully automated pipeline replaced human annotation entirely.
Quality checks confirmed that the automated labels aligned well with expert judgments.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experiments</h2>

<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.22570v1/agg_in_house_mean.svg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:471/171;" width="471" height="171"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>Average proof scores on CNML-level problems by category and model, as evaluated by our verifier.</figcaption>
</figure>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Training Settings</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employed Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for reinforcement learning, iteratively optimizing proof verification and generation capabilities as described in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 Method ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.
In each iteration, we first optimized proof verification. The proof generator was then initialized from the verifier checkpoint and optimized for proof generation.
Starting from the second iteration, the proof verifier was initialized with a checkpoint that consolidated both verification and generation capabilities from the previous iteration through rejection fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Evaluation Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our final proof generator on the following theorem proving benchmarks:</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">In-House CNML-Level Problems</span> 91 theorem-proving problems spanning algebra (13), geometry (24), number theory (19), combinatorics (24), and inequality (11), comparable in difficulty to problems from Chinese National High School Mathematics League (CNML)</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Competition Problems</span></p>
<ul id="S3.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">IMO 2025</span> (6 problems): The International Mathematical Olympiad, the premier global mathematics competition for pre-university students</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CMO 2024</span> (6 problems): The China Mathematical Olympiad, China’s national championship</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Putnam 2024</span> (12 problems): The William Lowell Putnam Competition, the preeminent mathematics competition for undergraduate students in North America</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ISL 2024</span> (31 problems): The IMO Shortlist, a collection of problems proposed by participating countries and considered by the Problem Selection Committee for potential inclusion in IMO 2024</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">IMO-ProofBench</span> (60 problems): Developed by the DeepMind team behind DeepThink IMO-Gold <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luong and Lockhart, 2025</a>)</cite>, this benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luong et al., 2025</a>)</cite> is divided into a basic set (30 problems, pre-IMO to IMO-Medium difficulty) and an advanced set (30 challenging problems simulating complete IMO examinations, up to IMO-Hard level)</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Evaluation Results</h3>

<section id="S3.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.1 </span>One-Shot Generation</h4>

<div id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first evaluate the model’s ability to generate correct proofs without iterative refinement.
On the in-house problems, we generated 8 proof samples per problem for each evaluated model.
Proof correctness was measured by majority voting across 8 verification analyses produced by our final verifier.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, across all categories of CNML-level problems – algebra, geometry, number theory, combinatorics, and inequality – DeepSeekMath-V2 consistently outperforms GPT-5-Thinking-High <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite> and Gemini 2.5-Pro <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepMind, 2025</a>)</cite>, demonstrating superior theorem-proving ability across domains.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.2 </span>Sequential Refinement with Self-Verification</h4>

<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_floatright" style="width:52%;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.22570v1/ISL2024_scores.svg" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:238/158;" width="238" height="158"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Proof quality improvements as the maximum sequential iterations varies from 1 (no refinement) to 8 (initial generation plus up to 7 refinements based on self verification).</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For challenging problems from competitions like IMO and CMO, models often cannot generate comprehensive and rigorous proofs in a single attempt within the 128K token limit.
When this occurs, our proof generator recognizes its proof is invalid through self-verification but lacks the context length to resolve all identified issues in a single attempt.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To explore how extended context and self-verification can improve proof quality, we evaluate sequential refinement with self-verification.
This approach first generates a proof with self-analysis, then iteratively re-prompts the generator with its previous output (see Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Proof Refinement Prompt ‣ Appendix A Prompt Templates ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a> for the refinement prompt), allowing it to address identified issues.
The process continues until the generator assigns itself a perfect score or reaches the maximum number of sequential attempts.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.3.2 Sequential Refinement with Self-Verification ‣ 3.3 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> demonstrates proof quality improvement through sequential refinement on IMO Shortlist 2024 problems.
For each problem, we launched 32 independent refinement threads.
Proof correctness was measured by majority voting across 32 verification analyses from our final verifier.
We report two metrics in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.3.2 Sequential Refinement with Self-Verification ‣ 3.3 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>: (1) Pass@1 – the average score of the final proof from each thread, and (2) Best@32 – the score of the best proof per problem, selected by self-assigned scores across all threads.
The self-selected best proofs achieve significantly higher verification scores than the thread average, demonstrating our generator’s ability to accurately assess proof quality.
Furthermore, Pass@1 improves substantially as maximum sequential attempts increase, showing that self-verification effectively guides iterative improvement.
These results confirm that our generator can reliably differentiate between high-quality and flawed proofs, and leverage this self-awareness to systematically improve its mathematical reasoning.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2511.22570v1/proofbench_bars.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:462/116;" width="462" height="116"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Expert evaluation results on the Basic and Advanced subsets of IMO-ProofBench. (2025)</a></cite>, with the exception of DeepSeekMath-V2, which was evaluated by our experts following the grading guidelines.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.3.3 </span>High-Compute Search</h4>

<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table ltx_align_floatright" style="width:52%;">

<td id="S3.T1.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t">73.8%</td></tr>

<td id="S3.T1.2.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">98.3%</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Problems in gray are <span id="S3.T1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-bg-color:#E6E6E6;">fully solved</span>, while underlined problems received <span id="S3.T1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_underline ltx_font_bold">partial credit</span>. </figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To solve the most challenging problems, we scaled both verification and generation compute – using extensive verification to identify subtle issues and parallel generation to explore diverse proof strategies.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our approach maintains a pool of candidate proofs for each problem, initialized with 64 proof samples with 64 verification analyses generated for each.
In each refinement iteration, we select the 64 highest-scoring proofs based on average verification scores and pair each with 8 randomly selected analyses, prioritizing those identifying issues (scores 0 or 0.5).
Each proof-analysis pair is used to generate one refined proof, which then updates the candidate pool.
This process continues for up to 16 iterations or until a proof successfully passes all 64 verification attempts, indicating high confidence in correctness.
All experiments used a single model, our final proof generator, which performs both proof generation and verification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To validate our results, mathematical experts assessed the highest-scoring proofs.
As shown in Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3.3 High-Compute Search ‣ 3.3 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, our approach solved 5 of 6 problems from IMO 2025 and 4 problems plus partial credit on another from CMO 2024, achieving gold medal performance in both pinnacle high-school competitions.
On Putnam 2024, the preeminent undergraduate mathematics competition, our model solved 11 of 12 problems completely and the remaining problem with minor errors, scoring 118/120 and surpassing the highest human score of 90.
Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 3.3.2 Sequential Refinement with Self-Verification ‣ 3.3 Evaluation Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ DeepSeekMath-V2: Towards Self-Verifiable Mathematical Reasoning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> shows the results on IMO-ProofBench.
Our approach outperforms DeepMind’s DeepThink (IMO Gold) on the basic set and remains competitive on the advanced set, while substantially outperforming all other baselines.
We observe that the hardest IMO-level problems remain challenging for our model.
Notably, for problems not fully solved, our generator typically identifies the genuine issues in its proofs, while fully solved problems pass all 64 verification attempts.
This demonstrates that we can successfully train LLM-based verifiers to assess proofs previously considered difficult to verify automatically.
By scaling test-time compute under verifier guidance, our model solves problems that require hours of effort from human competitors.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Reasoning models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025</a>)</cite> have saturated quantitative reasoning benchmarks like AIME and HMMT within one year.
This rapid advancement is partly attributed to the well-defined evaluation criterion: if we care only about final answers, then quantitative reasoning is easy to verify.
However, this final answer metric is inapplicable to theorem proving, which often requires no numerical answers but demands rigorous step-by-step derivation.
Informal mathematical proofs have long been considered hard to verify automatically, lacking reliable approaches to assess proof correctness.
Recent developments suggest this barrier may be surmountable.
Models like Gemini-2.5 Pro already demonstrate a certain level of self-verification capabilities, which can refine their own solutions to improve quality <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Huang and Yang, 2025</a>)</cite>.
More significantly, DeepMind’s internal DeepThink variant <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luong and Lockhart, 2025</a>)</cite> achieved gold medal performance at IMO 2025 using pure natural language reasoning – serving as an existence proof that LLM-based verification of complex proofs is achievable.
Recent research has begun exploring whether reasoning models can evaluate proofs, both with and without reference solutions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dekoninck et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Luong et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, showing promising results.
In this work, we open source DeepSeekMath-V2 and our training methodology as concrete steps toward self-verifiable mathematical reasoning, showing how models can learn to verify and improve their own proofs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Proof assistants like Lean <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">de Moura et al., 2015</a>)</cite> and Isabelle <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Paulson, 1994</a>)</cite> offer a reliable approach to verify proofs – proofs must be written in formal language, but once compiled, correctness is guaranteed.
AlphaProof <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">AlphaProof and teams, 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trinh et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chervonyi et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, a system specialized for formal proof search, achieved silver-level performance at IMO 2024 but required intensive computation.
While using informal reasoning to guide formal proof generation has been explored extensively <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, recent reasoning models have dramatically improved informal reasoning quality, making this guidance far more effective.
Systems like DeepSeek-Prover-V2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ren et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Seed-Prover <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> can now produce substantially more valid formal proofs within the same computational budget, with Seed-Prover solving 5 of 6 problems at IMO 2025.
Notably, these results were achieved without specifically optimizing the informal reasoning components for theorem proving tasks.
We believe advancing natural language theorem proving will significantly benefit formal reasoning.
We hope to contribute toward truly reliable mathematical reasoning systems that leverage both informal insights and formal guarantees to advance mathematical research.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We presented DeepSeekMath-V2, a model capable of both generating and verifying mathematical proofs.
By training models to identify issues in their own reasoning and incentivizing them to address these issues before finalizing outputs, we move beyond the limitations of final-answer-based rewards toward self-verifiable mathematical reasoning.
Our iterative training process – alternating between improving verification capabilities and using these to enhance generation – creates a sustainable cycle where each component drives the other forward.
Our key technical contributions include: (1) training an accurate and faithful LLM-based verifier for mathematical proofs, (2) using meta-verification to largely reduce hallucinated issues and ensure verification quality, (3) incentivizing the proof generator to maximize proof quality through self-verification, and (4) scaling verification compute to automatically label increasingly hard-to-verify proofs to improve the verifier without human annotation.
DeepSeekMath-V2 demonstrates strong performance on competition mathematics.
With scaled test-time compute, it achieved gold-medal scores in high-school competitions including IMO 2025 and CMO 2024, and a near-perfect score on the undergraduate Putnam 2024 competition.
This work establishes that LLMs can develop meaningful self-evaluation abilities for complex reasoning tasks.
While significant challenges remain, we hope this research direction contributes to the goal of creating self-verifiable AI systems that can solve research-level mathematics.</p>
</div>
</section>

    <h2>Instructions for reporting errors</h2>
    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"
            height="1em" viewBox="0 0 640 640">

              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>
    </ul>
    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
